records.name: Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF)
records.summary: The LDCF and SCFF are sister funds managed by the GEF to serve the Paris Agreement. The LDCF is the only facility exclusively dedicated to helping LDCs adapt to climate change. These channels support diverse activities including institutional strengthening, landscape restoration, and localized resilience-building. LDCF funding helps least developed countries address their short-, medium-, and long-term resilience needs and reduce climate change vulnerability in priority sectors and ecosystems.
records.intermediaries: The LDCF works through formally accredited GEF Agencies. Among them are UN agencies, multilateral and regional development banks, national government institutions, and international and non-governmental organisations.
records.capital: Public, based on voluntary contributions from developed country parties to the UNFCCC
records.countries: Least Developed Countries
records.frequency: Project applications are typically initiated by member countries based on their priorities and requirements on a rolling basis.
records.size: The total LDCF contribution for a Medium-Sized Project (MSP) cannot exceed USD 5 million. Beyond that, the project is considered a Full-Sized Project (FSP).
records.thematic: Climate change adaptation, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, economic recovery, health, industry and infrastructure, oceans and coasts, waste
records.targetGroups: Least developed countries
records.activities:
The LDCF works with partner agencies to bolster technical and institutional capacity at the national and local level, to create a policy environment that encourages investment in adaptation solutions, to reduce systemic barriers to progress, and to promote innovation and private sector engagement.

LDCF funding has addressed a range of adaptation priorities in the LDCs across a range of vulnerable sectors including agriculture, water, disaster risk management, coastal zone management, infrastructure, and sustainable alternate livelihoods among others. The GEF-8 adaptation strategy for the LDCF/SCCF aims to focus on agriculture, food security and health, water, climate information services, and nature-based solutions. The strategy aims to further support LDCs in addressing their adaptation priorities by scaling up access to adaptation finance, strengthen innovation and private sector engagement, and foster whole-of-society approach and partnerships for inclusion.
records.whoCanApply: Grants are accessible for national governments of least developed countries that are part of the UNFCCC.

records.name: Special Climate Change Fund
records.summary: The  SCFF and LDCF are sister funds managed by the GEF to serve the Paris Agreement and the climate adaptation efforts of developing countries. The SCCF  supports adaptation-focused technology transfer, innovation, and private sector engagement across all developing countries, apart from providing dedicated funding to support the climate adaptation needs of Small Island Developing States.
records.intermediaries: GEF Partners Agencies (GEF Agencies) are the only institutions that access GEF funding directly on behalf of an eligible recipient (government) for the design and implementation of GEF-financed projects. There are currently 18 GEF Agencies including UN agencies, multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, and NGOs. Projects can be executed on the ground by any organization, including private sector, civil society, government and non-governmental organizations.
records.capital: Public, based on voluntary contributions from developed country parties to the UNFCCC
records.countries: Non-Annex I Parties to the UNFCCC
records.frequency: Project applications are typically initiated by member countries based on their priorities and requirements on a rolling basis.
records.size: The total SCCF  contribution for a Medium-Sized Project (MSP) cannot exceed USD 5 million. Beyond that, the project is considered a Full-Sized Project (FSP). As of November 2024, the cumulative pledges to the Fund amount to approximately USD 460 million, with USD 422 million delivered to its trust fund.
records.thematic: Climate change adaptation, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, economic recovery, health, industry and infrastructure, jobs, nature based solutions and ecosystem services, oceans and coasts, waste, water, rural development
records.targetGroups: Non-annex 1 member countries UNFCCC, benefitting small businesses and small farmers among others
records.activities: Activities funded by the SCCF have fostered improvements in agriculture, water resources, disaster risk management, infrastructure, climate information systems, natural resource and integrated coastal zone management, as well as climate change-driven disease prevention. SCCF financing has also bolstered the climate resilience of public infrastructure such as schools, roads, and ports, supported the development of catastrophe risk insurance, and supported small and medium-sized enterprises and small farmers in the adaptation space.
records.whoCanApply: Grants are accessible for national governments of Non-Annex I Parties to the UNFCCC. The Fund gives priority to the most vulnerable countries to climate change.

records.name: BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (ISFL)
records.summary: The BioCarbon Fund (BCF), a World Bank multi-donor trust fund focused on forest carbon projects, supports REDD+ and sustainable landscape initiatives globally.The ISFL is a multilateral facility that promotes and rewards reduced greenhouse gas emissions and increased sequestration through better land management, including reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+), climate-smart agriculture, and smarter land-use planning and policies. It operates in developing countries, with current projects in Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Mexico, and Zambia.
records.intermediaries: World Bank (The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, acting as Trustee of the BioCarbon Fund T3 provides secretariat services through a Fund Management Team).
records.implementers: Implementing agencies can include national focal points, and other public entities at the national, sub-national and regional levels.
records.capital: Public-private partnership (PPP) managed by the World Bank. It receives funding from governments (e.g., Norway, UK, US, Germany, Switzerland—public donors providing the majority) and private entities (corporations and investors contributing alongside), blending public multilateral resources with private capital for carbon projects.
records.countries: Developing countries
records.frequency: Dependent on scoping, party negotiations and party readiness.
records.size: ISFL projects typically include grant funding between USD 15 to 40 million and results based payments ranging from USD 5 million to 40 million. Most projects currently running have been in the pipeline for around 10 years, since 2017/18.
records.thematic: Agriculture, food systems, forestry, biodiversity.
records.targetGroups:
Primarily targets rural communities, forest-dependent populations (including indigenous peoples and women), smallholder farmers, and forest-dwelling citizens in high-deforestation landscapes across participating countries. It aims to benefit over 500,000 people by 2030 through livelihood improvements, engaging national/sub-national governments, private sector actors (commodity producers, traders), and vulnerable groups via low-carbon rural economies that enhance agricultural productivity while protecting forests.

The ISFL program in Indonesia comprises the Jambi Sustainable Landscape Management Project (J-SLMP) and the Jambi Emission Reductions Results Program (J-ERRP) in the Jambi Province, with the former forming the foundation for the latter. Both aim to increase forest areas, improve sustainable land management, and reduce land-based GHG emissions in the region.
Key commodities and sectors include fisheries, livestock, palm oil, pulpwood (plantation-grown acacia and eucalyptus, planted in the natural forest areas after being harvested for pulpwood), rubber, robusta and arabica coffee (smallholder crops), rice, vegetables, fruit, coconut, cinnamon, soybean, areca nut, and cacao.
records.activities:
Reducing deforestation/degradation (REDD+) and promoting sustainable forest management.
Climate-smart agriculture practices like improved livestock management and supply chain greening.
Land-use planning/policy reforms to lower land-based GHG emissions (up to 30% globally).
Capacity building, benefit-sharing, and private sector engagement for low-carbon rural economies
records.whoCanApply: Via government/NGO partnerships and readiness programs; involves FPIC consultations and multi-stakeholder platforms for scaling national efforts

records.name: eco.business Fund
records.summary: The eco.business Fund is an impact investment fund that promotes biodiversity conservation and climate resilience by financing sustainable practices in nature-based businesses. It operates primarily in Latin America and Africa.
records.intermediaries: The Fund provides financing via financial institutions to ensure more businesses can access capital, besides investing directly in businesses. The Fund is managed by Finance in Motion (FiM) and was initiatied by FiM, KfW, and Conservation International.
records.capital: Blended, including public and private investors such as Germany, EU, UK, Norway, ASN Bank, and Calvert Impact.
records.instruments: Private debt (Senior loans, Subordinate loans, Mezzanine debt)
records.countries: Countries in Latin America and the Caribbean and Africa
records.frequency: The selection process appears to be internally led.
records.size: Unclear
records.thematic: Agriculture, forestry, aquaculture and tourism
records.targetGroups:
The fund aims to increase financing for​:

Commercial banks​
Agricultural Cooperatives​
Agribusinesses ​
Aquaculture businesses ​
Agricultural intermediaries​
Food value chain companies
records.activities:
Target activities include:
Strengthening Environmental and Social Management Systems (“ESMS”)
Future-proofing businesses, e.g. by strengthening Environmental and Social Management Systems (“ESMS”)
Broadening product offering and revenue streams, e.g. by helping structure sustainable financial products
Improving market visibility, e.g. by exchanging knowledge resources, training sponsorship and event access
records.keywords: Agricultural Cooperatives​, Agribusinesses​, Aquaculture businesses, smallholders
records.whoCanApply: The fund aims to ultimately benefit agricultural cooperatives, businesses and intermediaries, but since financing is provided via financial institutions, it may not be directly accessible to these groups.

records.name: Global Youth Climate Action Fund (GYCAF)
records.summary: The Global Youth Climate Action Fund (GYCAF) is the first of its kind climate fund dedicated to financing youth-led climate action around the world. GYCAF provides direct funding, training, and mentorship to youth-led initiatives that deliver measurable environmental and social impact, including in the sustainable agriculture sector.
records.intermediaries: The Fund is hosted by BLI Global. Partners include foundations, philanthropies, grassroots youth  organizations worldwide, youth-led platforms and networks.
records.implementers: Projects are implemented directly by grantees.
records.capital: Blended, including private (corporate social responsibility and impact-driven funding) and philanthropic.
records.countries: Global
records.frequency: Calls appear to be issued annually and are usually open for four weeks.
records.size: Grant size is between USD 500 - USD 1,000
records.thematic: Sustainable Agriculture, Clean Energy, Oceans, Biodiversity, Technology and Innovation
records.targetGroups: Communities vulnerable to climate change impacts
records.activities:
GYCAF provides direct funding, training, and mentorship to youth-led initiatives that deliver measurable environmental and social impact in the following sectors:

Sustainable Agriculture: smart agriculture to ensure food sustainability.
Clean Energy: powering communities in need of light and energy.
Oceans: protecting marine life and mitigating climate catastrophes.
Capacity Building: empowering youth with entrepreneurship skills.
Green Stewardship: protecting biodiversity and influencing behavioral change.
Technology and Innovation: breakthroughs that solve climate-related problems.
records.whoCanApply: Young individuals and youth organizations, community-based organizations and business ventures can apply.

records.name: Mobilising Finance For Forests (MFF) Program
records.summary: The MFF program is a blended finance investment program to combat deforestation and other environmentally unsustainable land use practices in tropical regions in Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa.
records.intermediaries: The MFF program is funded by the UK and Netherlands governments.
records.implementers: The Dutch development bank FMO is the implementing agency of this program.
records.capital: Blended. While the MFF comprises public funds (EUR 178 million (GBP 150 million) from the UK government), the objective is to mobilize private finance (EUR 1 billion) for forestry and sustainable land use projects through catalytic investments.
records.countries: Tropical countries in Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa
records.frequency: The selection process does not appear to be call-based.
records.size:
MFF offers long term financing up to 15 years to a mix of fund and direct investments.  Up to 20% of the funding can be used for early stage project development.

Fund investments in 3 to 5 Funds (70-80% of the program):
Investment funds targeting sustainable investments in the forestry and other land-use sectors
Equity or debt investments
Direct investments (20-30% of program)
Minority shares in equity investments
Loans of up to (the equivalent of) EUR 10 million
records.thematic: nature-based solutions to tackle the drivers of climate change and biodiversity loss, protect and restore critical ecosystems; build resilience, just rural transition towards sustainable land use
records.targetGroups: Fund managers, companies with forest-related projects
records.activities:
The MFF targets:
- Projects that increase the value of standing forests to lower the incentive to cut down forests (e.g. harvesting non-timber forest products such as nuts, seeds or native forest coffee, carbon offsetting schemes, eco tourism, conservation projects).
- Projects that integrate forest protection and restoration into agricultural production to reduce deforestation pressure (e.g soy, cattle, palm oil, cocoa, timber).
records.whoCanApply: Investments are directed at fund managers and companies engaged in forest-related projects.

records.name: Alterfin
records.summary: Alterfin is a Belgian social co-operative that offers investment opportunities to generate a positive social, environmental and economic impact. Since 1994, Alterfin has been financing social enterprises in Latin-America, Africa and Asia that support farmers and entrepreneurs in generating sustainable incomes.
records.intermediaries: None.
records.implementers: Alterfin works with target groups (local microfinance instititutions and sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations) directly.
records.capital: Private. Co-operative members' investment through shares. Alterfin has over 5700 individuals and organizations as cooperative members.
records.countries: Latin-American, African and Asian countries
records.frequency: rolling basis
records.size: Finance is provided between USD 100,000 and USD 1,500,000. For agricultral organizations, this can be in the form of short-term loans (3-12 months, for financing harvests) or long-term loans (up to five years to finance fixed assets).
records.thematic: Sustainable agriculture, climate change adaptation, poverty reduction, improving rural livelihoods, gender equality
records.targetGroups: Sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations (including cooperatives and small and medium-sized agricultural enterprises) and microfinance institutions
records.activities:
Financial services: providing short- and long-term loans for microfinance institutions and agricultural SMEs to finance their working capital.
‍
Non-financial services: financing technical assistance projects
records.keywords: Sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations (including cooperatives and small and medium-sized agricultural enterprises) and microfinance institutions
records.whoCanApply: The loans can be accessed by co-operatives and small- and medium-sized agricultural enterprises, and other smallholder organizations, besides microfinance institutions.

records.name: Global Fund for Coral Reefs
records.summary: As an implementation vehicle for the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and Sustainable Development Goal 14 (SDG 14), Life Below Water, the Global Fund for Coral Reefs (GFCR) coalition strengthens the resilience of coastal reef ecosystems, local communities, and economies by mobilising new public and private resources that advance sustainable businesses and innovative financial solutions. GFCR’s locally driven implementation and investments follow an integrated ecosystem-based approach focused on “coral refugia,” coral reef habitats that demonstrate resilience to climate change impacts.
records.programme: GCFR UN Fund and GCFR Equity Fund
records.programmeSummary: The GFCR deploys resources through two main instruments – a GFCR UN Fund and a GFCR Equity Fund. The GFCR UN Fund focuses on building an enabling environment for market-based investment in businesses and financial mechanisms aligned to the GFCR conservation aims. The GFCR Equity Fund, managed by Pegasus Capital Advisors (PCA), builds upon the enabling environment by investing in large impact deals that can leverage significant capital for reef-positive businesses.
records.intermediaries: The fund is managed by a UN Global Team and provides finance through GCFR's on-site partners. These include international and national conservation and sustainable investment leaders who provide incubation services and pipeline development for enterprises, finance mechanisms, and other solutions at country and regional levels. In addition to co-founding the GFCR, the three UN agencies play a core role in convening the public-private coalition, the UN Capital Development Fund, UNDP and UNEP. Other strategic partners include the Catalytic FInance Foundation, Conservation Finance Alliance, Blue Nature Alliance, Race to Resilience, UNESCO and Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance.  Overall, at the global level, the GFCR is powered by a Coalition comprised of Member States, UN Agencies, financial institutions, philanthropies, impact investors, and conservation organisations.
records.implementers: Key implementing partners can include national and local NGOs, universities, corporations (including banks), marine protected area management authroiries, and conservation alliances or other funded programmes.
records.capital: Blended. Includes philanthropic (e.g. Bloomberg Philanthropies and Allen Family Philanthropies), public (e.g. UK, US, Norway, Germany) and private sector (e.g. ICONIQ Impact) funds.
records.instruments: grants, technical assistance, and concessional finance through payment for ecosystem services (e.g. blue carbon, coral reef insurance, biodiversity credits), debt conversion, bonds, and conservation trust funds
records.countries: Coral countries
records.frequency: More than 130 reef-positive businesses and finance solutions received GFCR support between 2020 and 2024. In 2024, 8 national and regional programs were also approved for funding. The selection process is not based on advertised calls, but appears to be led in collaboration with national and local partners.
records.size: 8 jurisdictional/seascape projects were approved in 2024, with funding ranging from USD 0.8 million to 15 million, with most projects receving financing between USD 2-5 million.
records.initiative:
Blue Alliance Loan Facility for coral reef conservation:
One distinctive pathway within the GFCR portfolio is the vertically integrated model developed by Blue Alliance. Unlike other programmes where enterprise development and financing roles are distributed across separate entities, Blue Alliance acts simultaneously as a business incubator, impact investor, and MPA co-manager. In 2024,  Blue Alliance secured USD 2.4 million in anchor investment from BNP Paribas to launch the first Impact Loan Facility for coral reef conservation. This facility provides flexible debt financing for the aquaculture, ecotourism, and fisheries businesses that Blue Alliance is incubating in co-management areas.

Another instrument is the Coral Reef Funding Facility (CRRF), designed by YKAN Indonesia, which is a reimbursable grant mechanism, i.e. a flexible instrument positioned to address the “valley of death” in enterprise development.
records.thematic: reef conservation and resilience, sustainable livelihoods
records.targetGroups: Commercial projects and businesses, to benefit local communities
records.activities: Target activities include but are not limited to sustainable fisheries, seaweed mariculture, and sustainable marine ecotourism.
records.whoCanApply: The Fund targets commercial projects and therefore may not be suitable for non-corporate farmer organizations.

records.name: Forest Carbon Partnership Facility
records.summary: The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) is a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society, and Indigenous Peoples focused on REDD+ activities, supporting them through its Readiness Fund (2008 - 2022) and Carbon Fund. As the Carbon Fund also enters its last phase, community support is being carried forward with the EnABLE Fund.
records.programme: FCPF Carbon Fund
records.programmeSummary: The FCPF Carbon Fund pilots results-based payments to countries that have advanced through REDD+ readiness and implementation and have achieved verifiable emission reductions in their forest and broader land-use sectors. It operates in developing countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
records.intermediaries: The Fund leverages global partnerships built through the FCPF with governments, the private sector, civil society, international organizations, and Indigenous Peoples.
records.implementers: Delivery partners include World Bank, FAO, UNDP. Examples of implementing entities include national environment ministries.
records.capital: Blended, with several public donors including national governments like the US, UK, France, Norway and the European Commission and private donors like BP, and nonprofit donors like the Nature Conservancy.
records.countries: Countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
records.frequency: Dependent on scoping, party negotiations and party readiness.
records.size:
The FCPF has over 15 Emission Reductions Payment Agreements (ERPAs) with contract values ranging from USD 12 million (Fiji) to 100 million (Indonesia), with most being in the range of USD 40-50 million. ERPAs were mostly signed between 2018 and 2021, and 10 countries have already received payments inlcuding  FCPF Carbon Fund payments to
purchase verified emission reductions and advance payments.
records.thematic: Climate change mitigation related to forest loss and degradation
records.targetGroups: National governments, private sector, local communities, Indigenous Peoples
records.activities: Emission reductions programs take a jurisdiction-level approach toward engaging actors in agriculture, energy, transport, land, mining, and forestry to achieve climate-smart land use, protect forests, restore degraded land, and improve local livelihoods.
records.whoCanApply: National governments are the recipients of funds.

records.name: Forest Carbon Partnership Facility
records.summary: The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) is a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society, and Indigenous Peoples focused on REDD+ activities, supporting them through its Readiness Fund (2008 - 2022) and Carbon Fund. As the Carbon Fund also enters its last phase, community support is being carried forward with the EnABLE Fund.
records.programme: Enhancing Access to Benefits while Lowering Emissions (EnABLE) Fund
records.programmeSummary: In recent years the Carbon Fund has been supported by the EnABLE Fund, which provides global knowledge, operations, and technical assistance through direct financing to local implementing civil society organizations (CSOs). It thus facilitates access to climate finance for underrepresented groups in countries where the World Bank supports emission reductions programs (ERPs).
records.intermediaries: World Bank, FCPF
records.implementers: The majority of country-level activities are jointly executed by World Bank teams and local civil society organizations (CSOs).
records.capital: Blended. EnABLE’s initial programming has focused on 14 Carbon Fund countries under the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF). In Fiscal Year 2025, EnABLE received a new contribution to support social inclusion programs under the World Bank’s Scaling Climate Action by Lowering Emissions (SCALE) umbrella program.
records.countries: Countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
records.frequency: The Fund undertakes targeted stakeholder engagement, including the identification of local CSOs with the appropriate networks, capacity, and experience to engage with target communities to implement EnABLE’s programming.
records.size: The size of the small grants provided is unclear.
records.thematic: access to climate finance
records.targetGroups:
Local civil society groups representing or working with historically marginalized and disadvantaged groups, especially forest-dependent Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and traditional local communities (LCs).

Vulnerable groups within these communities, including women and girls, children and youth, and people living in poverty and with disabilities.
records.activities:
EnABLE supports social inclusion in climate finance initiatives through interventions such as:
- Extending grants to relevant civil society and community-based organizations to undertake locally led, scalable initiatives that raise awareness of emission reductions programs and benefit sharing plans among target groups and build their capacity to engage in and benefit from such programs (examples include supporting meaningful communication, promoting tenure security, implementing community program monitoring systems, and promoting equitable transitions)
- Providing technical assistance and small grants supporting enabling policy environments and legal frameworks; diversifying skills; piloting activities on sustainable resource management, the adoption and expansion of clean energy sources, and alternative (low-carbon) livelihoods; and building climate and livelihood resilience among targeted communities and groups
- Supporting the exchange of insights into and experiences of results-based climate finance, including establishing and supporting peer-to-peer networks for target groups
records.keywords: forest-dependent Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and traditional local communities, which could potentially include farmer organizations. Indigenous family agriculture   supported.
records.whoCanApply: Funds can be accessed by CSOs representing forest-dependent Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and traditional local communities, which could potentially include organizations representing farmers.

records.name: UNDP Direct Grants for Indigenous Peoples (Climate Promise)
records.summary: The Direct Grants mechanism is supported by UNDP with funding from DEFRA (UK), BMZ (Germany), and the UN-REDD Programme. Communities use grants to protect forests, formalize land rights, resolve conflicts, and invest in sustainable livelihoods rooted in traditional knowledge. It is associated with the Climate Promise initiative, under which UNDP delivers the UN system’s largest portfolio of support on climate action in more than 140 countries and territories.
records.intermediaries: UNDP provides funding directly to community grantees.
records.implementers: Projects are implemented by indigenous and local community groups with support from local NGOs and the UNDP.
records.capital: Public.  DEFRA (UK), BMZ (German), and the UN-REDD Programme
records.countries: Ecuador, Colombia, Kenya and Cambodia (implementation so far)
records.frequency: Unclear, but may operate through regularly posted calls for applications by UNDP or selection with the support of national and local partners.
records.size: While individual grant size is unclear, UNDP has provided 51 grants to 42 Indigenous communities in Ecuador, Colombia, Kenya and Cambodia worth a total of USD 1.8 million since 2023.
records.thematic: climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity conservation, Indigenous Peoples’ rights and sovereignty
records.targetGroups: Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities
records.activities:
A key priority is to provide Indigenous Peoples and local communities with the autonomy to identify their priorities, design and implement solutions to climate change and biodiversity loss rooted in their cultural and environmental knowledge.
For example, between 2024 and 2025, Indigenous communities across six provinces in Cambodia used grants to protect forests, formalize land rights, resolve conflicts and strengthen sustainable livelihoods. Across project sites, communities followed their own plans to embrace agroecology and agroforestry practices, develop alternative livelihoods, strengthen leadership structures and enhance financial management. Indigenous savings groups, cattle banks, vegetable gardens, and small enterprises are support daily needs while reducing pressure on forest resources.
records.keywords: Indigenous savings groups, small enterprises, small-scale agriculture
records.whoCanApply: Funds are directly provided to indigenous and local community groups, which could include small-scale farmer and producer organizations.

records.name: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund
records.summary: This funding opportunity supports civil society-led initiatives in the Indo-Burma region that strengthen protected area governance, integrate biodiversity into development planning, and build the capacity of local organizations, with grants ranging from USD 50,000 to USD 250,000.
records.intermediaries: See Capital Source.
records.implementers:
CEPF's regional implementation teams work in the biodiversity hotspots with CEPF’s grantees, helping to build local capacity and implement CEPF’s conservation strategy. These include:
- Caribbean Islands: Caribbean Natural Resources Institute (CANARI)
- Indo-Burma: IUCN Asia Regional office
- Madagascar and Indian Ocean islands: IUCN NL, SAF/FJKM (Madagascar), ID (Comoros), FORENA (Mauritius) and SeyCCAT (Seychelles)
- Mediterranean Basis: BirdLife International, DOPPS - BirdLife Slovenia
- Mountains of Central Asia: Fund for the Conservation of Rare Species of Animals and Plants
- Tropical Andes: Profonanpe, Fondo Patrimonio Natural, ACEAA - Conservación Amazónica
- Tropical Andes, Ecuador: Fundación Futuro Latinoamericano (FFLA)
- Wallacea: Burung Indonesia
records.capital: Blended, including public and philanthropic donors. CEPF is a joint initiative of l’Agence Française de Développement, Conservation International, the European Union, Fondation Hans Wilsdorf, the Global Environment Facility, the Government of Canada, the Government of Japan and the World Bank.
records.countries:
CEPF currently works in the following areas:
Caribbean Islands
Guinean Forests of West Africa
Indo-Burma
Madagascar and Indian Ocean Islands
Mediterranean Basin
Mountains of Central Asia
Tropical Andes
Wallacea
records.frequency: Calls for proposals are open several times for each hotspot where CEPF is active (0-3 calls per year per hotspot).
records.size:
Small grants (up to USD 50,000, on average USD 15,000) and large grants (USD 50,000 to 250,000, on average USD 150,000). Grants more than USD 500,000 are awarded only in exceptional cases.

Funded projects are usually 1-2 years in length, and large grants may be for longer periods where needed.
records.thematic: biodiversity, livelihoods, nature-based solutions
records.targetGroups: Indigenous People and Local Communities
records.activities:
Target activities include:
- conserving species in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
- strengthening management and protection of Key Biodiversity Areas
- establishing new protected areas
- improved management of production landscapes, i.e. areas where agriculture, forestry or natural product harvesting occurs
- community benefits including improved access to clean water, improved land tenure and increased representation in decision-making processes.
records.keywords: farmers' cooperatives, small businesses, and other local civil society organisations (CSOs), smallholder farmers
records.whoCanApply: Non-governmental organisations, community groups, Indigenous People’s organisations, women’s groups, private companies, small businesses, farmers' cooperatives and other local civil society organisations (CSOs) can apply if legally registered. This could include small-scale farmer and producer organizations.

records.name: Canadian Climate and Nature Fund for the Private Sector in Asia
records.summary: This fund established by the Canadian government aims to stimulate private sector investment in climate and nature-based solutions (NbS) projects that advance gender equality across Asia and the Pacific, especially in developing countries and small island developing states.
records.intermediaries: The fund is financed by the Government of Canada through Global Affairs Canada.
records.implementers: ADB is the trustee and manager of the fund.
records.capital: Public.
records.instruments: Concessional debt instruments, including senior and subordinated loans, mezzanine financing (debt) instruments, and guarantees
records.countries: Asian and Pacific countries, especially developing countries and small island developing states.
records.frequency: Not open for direct applications by farmer groups.
records.size: The total fund size is CAD 360 million. ADB will deploy capital over a 7-year investment period followed by an implementation period of up to 20 years. ADB will blend the fund’s resources with its ordinary capital resources.
records.thematic: clean energy,NbS and biodiversity, climate-smart agriculture, climate governance
records.targetGroups: Private enterprises working with NbS, including MSMEs
records.activities:
Target activities include:
(i) reducing emissions and transitioning away from high carbon pathways to improve resilience to climate change;
(ii) financing NbS to protect, sustainably manage, and restore natural or modified ecosystems.
This includes:
Habitat restoration and protection
Sustainable aquaculture
Sustainable (climate-smart) agriculture
Pollution prevention and water management
Nature protection and ecotourism
records.keywords: micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), including MSMEs owned and/or led by women (WMSMEs).

records.name: WALD Innovation Facility
records.summary: The Innovation Facility is a grant-making programme targeting new types of nature-based carbon projects that, due to their innovative nature, do not yet receive sufficient finance via the Voluntary Carbon Market, and make them investable for the private sector.  Projects funded focus on nature-based activities that sequester CO2 from the atmosphere, combined with strong positive biodiversity impacts, including forest restoration, agroforestry, carbon removal from peatlands and from blue carbon ecosystems.
records.intermediaries: German Federal Ministry of Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), KfW Development Bank, International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)
records.implementers: The Facility is managed and implemented by IUCN.
records.capital: Public.The Facility is funded by the German Federal Ministry of Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) via KfW Development Bank.
records.countries: ODA-eligible countries
records.frequency: One call for proposals has been issued so far, in 2025.
records.size: Grants range from EUR 750,000 to 1.5 million. The Innovation Facility requires grantees to provide match funding that amounts to at least 25% of the grant amount.
records.thematic: Nature-based solutions, biodiversity, climate change mitigation, forests, agroforestry, blue carbon, peatlands, livelihoods
records.targetGroups: New types of nature-based carbon projects that work closely with national stakeholders, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities
records.activities:
It is expected that the grant financing will be used for the final stage of project preparation and first concrete action on implementation, e.g. tree planting. The Innovation Facility aims to:

- Demonstrate that ambitious approaches can be scaled-up by mobilising private sector investments.
- Mitigate climate change and deliver positive impacts both on biodiversity and on people’s livelihoods.
- Support the application of new approaches and technologies to better and more efficiently measure and monitor the positive impacts on biodiversity.
records.whoCanApply:
The following groups may apply, if they have the technical, managerial and financial capacity to manage and implement high-quality nature-based carbon projects on the ground:

Local or international non-governmental organisations (NGOs)
Indigenous Peoples, and Local Communities
Project developers
Forestry and agricultural companies
Cooperatives
Other entities with the respective expertise.

records.name: Canada Fund for Local Initiatives
records.summary: The Canada Fund for Local Initiatives (CFLI) is a program designed to support small-scale, high-impact projects in developing countries, which align with Global Affairs Canada’s thematic priority areas for engagement. Targetted calls are issued for specific countries regularly.
records.intermediaries: The CLFI funds local organizations that develop small-scale and high-impact projects. Local organizations plan and carry out projects, while the Canadian Embassy or High Commission selects and approves them.
records.capital: Public. The programme is funded by the Canadian government.
records.countries: Over 120 ODA-eligible developing countries
records.frequency: The CFLI funds approximately 650 projects annually through country-specific calls.
records.size: The average CFLI contribution is CAD 15,000 to 30,000 Canadian Dollars (CAD 100,000 is the maximum allocation amount for a project eligible under CFLI). Project duration may be upto 1 year.
records.thematic: environmental and climate action, inclusive governance, peace and security
records.targetGroups: Local civil society organizations and other local insititutions
records.activities:
Activities should pertain to at least one of the thematic foci of the programme mentioned in the scope, as announced in each country-specific call. Thematic foci relevant to the agri-food sector include:
- Gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.
- Growth that benefits everyone, such as women's economic rights, fair jobs, and entrepreneurship, investing in the most vulnerable, and protecting economic progress.
- Environmental and climate action, focusing on adaptation and mitigation, and water management.
- Human dignity, covering health, education and nutrition.
records.keywords: local organizations that develop small-scale and high-impact projects. Could potentially include an agrifood focus.
records.whoCanApply:
Eligible recipients include:

Local non-governmental, community and not-for-profit organizations,
Local academic institutions working on local projects,
International non-governmental organizations working on local development activities,
Intergovernmental, multilateral and regional institutions, organizations and agencies working on local development activities,
Municipal, regional or national government institutions or agencies of the recipient country working on local projects, and
Canadian non-governmental and not-for-profit organizations that are working on local development activities.

Only those proposals using the designated application form and including the required budget document will be considered.

records.name: ResponsAbility Investments AG
records.summary: responsAbility is a Swiss impact asset manager specializing in private market investments across three investment themes: Financial Inclusion (to finance the growth of Micro & SMEs); Climate Finance, and Sustainable Food. responsAbility also offers tailor-made and fund investment solutions to institutional investors.
records.intermediaries: ResponsAbility invests equity in or lends directly to companies or invests in other investment funds.
records.capital: Private.
records.instruments: Private debt, private equity, fund investments
records.countries: Global ( around 70 countries with emerging markets)
records.frequency: Investments appear to be made through an internal selection process.
records.size: Funding size and length are unclear. As of 31 December 2025, the company managed USD 5.8 billion in assets across approximately 330 portfolio companies in around 70 countries.
records.thematic: Financial inclusion, sustainable food, climate finance
records.targetGroups: Microfinance institutions, early-stage micro, small and medium enterprises, and fund managers, with an emphasis on consumer mid-market private equity and late-stage venture capital funds
records.activities:
Target investments in the agri-food sector include:
- Companies that value smallholders, support their education, enable them with technology and pay them appropriately
- Sustainable processing and distribution, including essential value chain players, e.g. logistics, export, retail market
- Organic production and fair trade certifications
- Other agriculture value chain investments, e.g. in companies who provide credit to farmers and small and medium-sized companies across the value chain, organic supply chain management companies, farm-to-table food companies
- Climate smart agriculture, e.g. drip-irrigation, high-tech weather-monitoring and harvesting
records.keywords: smallholders, microfinance institutions, early-stage micro, small and medium enterprises
records.whoCanApply: The Fund is not open for direct applications.

records.name: Ocean Resilience and Coastal Adaptation Trust Fund (ORCA-TF)
records.summary: The ORCA-TF focusses on upstream planning, project preparation and capacity development for implementing investments in ocean health and coastal adaptation, with a focus on nature-based solutions, ecosystem management and restoration in Asia and the Pacific.
records.intermediaries: The Fund is administered by the ADB.
records.capital: Blended, with intent to mobilize both public and private finance. The ORCATF was established with USD 13 million in grant commitments from the Nordic Development Fund and UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. The Blue Pacific Finance Hub has leveraged an additional USD 10 million from the GEF Least Developed Countries Fund and more is anticipated.
records.countries: East Asia and Pacific countries
records.frequency: Project origination may occur through ADB country offices, governments, regional cooperation hubs, or through direct invitations to apply.
records.size: Active projects have received funding between USD 0.5 to 2 million for a duration of 3-6 years.
records.initiative: The ORCATF has a Pacific window and an Asia Window to support project origination through regional approaches such as the Blue Pacific Finance Hub and, for the Southeast Asia Department, complementary support to the Blue Southeast Asia (SEA) Finance Hub’s activities.
records.thematic: oceans, nature-based solutions, ecosystem restoration, food security
records.targetGroups: ADB member countries with eligibility to apply, benefitting fishers and fish workers, especially marginalized groups
records.activities: The ORCATF provides grant finance for ocean-positive project origination and preparation in all areas that contribute to measurable ocean health and resilience with a focus on nature-based solutions, ecosystem management and restoration. Activities should be integrated with ocean- and coastal-related components of national plans and commitments, such as nationally determined contributions and national adaptation plans, finance frameworks and fiscal policies, and environmental tax reform. Projects that can demonstrate they enhance donor co-ordination and/or facilitate new source of private sector finance will be prioritised.
records.keywords: inclusive livelihoods benefitting marginalized communities, women, small and medium-sized enterprises working on sustainable use of ocean and coastal resources
records.whoCanApply: Developing member countries eligible for support from the ORCATF include all those that border the ocean, a sea, or a major river that drains to the ocean. Initial priority countries include Cambodia, India, the Maldives, the Marshall Islands, Tonga and Vietnam.

records.name: Adaptation Benefits Mechanism
records.summary: The ABM is an innovative mechanism to will de-risk and incentivize public and private investments by facilitating payments for delivery of Adaptation Benefits. ABM will certify the social, economic and environmental benefits of adaptation activities. The value of adaptation action captured in these certificates (Certified Adaptation Benefits or CABs), including the incremental costs of generating the benefits, will be promoted to potential investors or lenders.  The pilot stage was concluded in late 2025 and the mechanism is now in a transition phase that will lead to the establishment of a permanent Secretariat by 2027. ABM is expected to be accomapnied with the creation of the African Adaptation Benefit Fund, which will finance the purchase of CABs to kick-start the ABM.
records.entityType: International results-based mechanism (Non-market approach under Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement)
records.intermediaries: The African Development Bank continues to be the lead incubator of the ABM as of 2026. the ABM was developed under the guidance of the AfDB in collaboration with African and international stakeholders, including countries like Uganda, with pilots in 13 African countries from 2019 to 2025 such as Benin, Nigeria, Kenya, Madagascar, Gambia and Guinea who are also listed as paritcipating parties in the UNFCCC Art. 6.8 Non market approaches platform.
records.capital:
Blended. The following funding roles are envisaged for the next phase of the ABM's development:
- Public finance can be utilized to de-risk early-stage projects and guarantee initial Certified Adaptation Benefits (CAB) purchases; grant funded projects can then be replicated by CAB buyers using the ex post financing model.
- Private and Institutional finance can develop capital market instruments to fund adaptation projects
- Emitters, private impact investors, ESG, CSR and corporate buyers can acquire CABs to demonstrate leadership in adaptation and manage supply chain risks within their sustainability portfolios.
- Development finance institutions can replenish grant funds and integrate CABs into loan and grant programs to better achieve adaptation outcomes.
- Philanthropic foundations can use CABs to ensure accountability and traceability of funded adaptation outcomes.
records.instruments: Certified Adaptation Benefits (a new asset class that transforms adaptation outputs and outcomes into quantified, verified and monetized assets, facilitating access to capital markets).  The price of a CAB is set to overcome the financial barriers in adaptation activities. All funds spent on purchasing a CAB are directed entirely to the project developer, to address these financial barriers. It includes ex-ante CABs (generated from existing adaptation projects) and ex-post CABs (from new projects, enabling developers to secure upfront financing based on expected verified results and CAB issuance). Future CAB revenues are guaranteed through an Adaptation Benefit Supply Agreement (ABSA).
records.countries: Global
records.frequency: Not applicable
records.size: Project dependent. For example, a pilot in Senegal concerning a 200 ha agroforestry project was priced at USD 300,000, with an 8-month monitoring period, and 5-year activity and benefits duration.
records.thematic: agricultural innovation, urban resilience, ecosystem restoration, climate-smart infrastructure
records.targetGroups: households, communities, economies
records.activities: Target adaptation benefits in the agri-food sector include: small-scale agro processing solutions, climate smart agriculture, agricultural insurance, small or large scale irrigation, and reduced deforestation and degradation (REDD+).
records.keywords: small-scale agro processing solutions, MSMEs, communities, cooperatives
records.whoCanApply: ABM activity developers could be private sector entities, including MSMEs, communities, cooperatives, NGOs, local authorities and others. They can generate CABs by submitting eligible ABM activities to the ABM Secretariat for approval by an independent ABM Executive Committee

records.name: Blue Planet Fund
records.summary: The Blue Planet Fund is a GBP 500 million portfolio of programmes funded by the UK government supporting developing countries to protect the marine environment and reduce poverty.
records.intermediaries: The programme is implemented by the UK government.
records.capital: Public, through the UK government, from the Official Development Assistance (ODA) budget.
records.countries:
ODA-eligible coastal countries across the following 6 priority regions:

South and Southeast Asia
West Africa
East Africa
Latin America
Caribbean Small Island Developing States (SIDS)
Pacific SIDS
records.frequency: Only some sub-programmes have directly accessible funding modalities.
records.size: Sub-programme/project dependent.
records.thematic: biodiversity, climate change, marine pollution, sustainable seafood
records.targetGroups: coastal communities
records.activities:
Across its thematic areas of biodiversity, climate change, marine pollution and sustainable seafood, the Blue Planet Fund has 7 outcomes it aims to support:
- Small scale fisheries management: Local communities have improved fisheries management knowledge, capacities and incentives, supporting more climate resilient, inclusive and sustainable livelihoods.
- Critical marine habitats for coastal resilience: Locally inclusive approaches that protect, sustainably manage and restore marine ecosystems are demonstrated, scaled, and financed with private sector support, leading to improved biodiversity, ecosystem services and climate resilience of coastal communities.
- Aquaculture: Sustainable, inclusive aquaculture approaches that help restore and avoid harm to the environment are demonstrated and increasingly adopted with private sector support.
- Marine protected areas (MPAs) and Other Effective Conservation Measures (OECMs)
- Illegal Unregulated and Unreported (IUU) fishing
- International and large-scale fisheries
- Solid waste and other forms of marine pollution

Programmes also incorporate cross-cutting themes such as gender and vulnerable groups, human rights and modern slavery, rule of law and corruption, nature based solutions, and economic shocks.
records.whoCanApply: Accessibility depends on the nature of the sub-programmes, e.g. bilateral and some multilateral funding is usually directed at national or sub-national governments, while there are some direct community funding mechanisms as well.

records.programme: Ocean Community Empowerment and Nature (OCEAN) Grants Programme
records.programmeSummary: The OCEAN Grants Programme is a global competitive grants initiative part of the Blue Planet Fund that supports a wide range of projects that work to protect the marine environment and reduce poverty. Proposals from in-country organisations that work directly with coastal communities are particularly encouraged. OCEAN comprises an investment of up to GBP 60 million from 2024 until 2029.
records.intermediaries: Applications and grants are administered by the consultancy NIRAS (referred to as ‘OCEAN Grants Administrator’).
records.capital: Public. OCEAN is funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), through the Blue Planet Fund.
records.countries: Eligible coastal least developed countries and lower middle income and upper middle income countries
records.frequency: The 5-year programme (2024-2029) has had two funding rounds until early 2026.
records.size:
Projects must last a minimum of 12 months, and multi-year projects are preferred.
Maximum Project Length: Up to 31 March 2029

Community grants up to GBP 250,000: small to medium, local, in-country organisations with annual income under GBP 1 million.

Partnership grants GBP 500,000 -  3 million: medium to large organisations who partner with locally led organisations and have the capacity to deliver projects at scale.

The annual value of any grant application should not be 50% more than of the lead organisation’s annual income for Community Grants and 25% for Partnership Grants.
records.thematic: marine environment protection and sustianable management, livelihoods in coastal communities, climate change mitigation and adaptation
records.targetGroups: coastal communities, local organizations
records.activities:
OCEAN funds projects that:
- support a reduction in multi-dimensional poverty
- focus on the protection, restoration, conservation or sustainable management of the marine environment
- demonstrate how they contribute to climate adaptation and/or climate mitigation.
records.keywords: small businesses, women-led fishing groups and cooperatives
records.whoCanApply:
Applications are welcomed from Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), private sector organisations, businesses, and business associations, especially in-country organisations that work directly with coastal communities.

Government agencies and inter-governmental organisations are not eligible to receive funding from OCEAN, but are highly encouraged to partner with local non-profit organisations to support their projects.

records.name: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR)
records.summary: The GFDRR is a global partnership that helps developing countries better understand and reduce their vulnerability to natural hazards and climate change. It is a grant-funding mechanism managed by the World Bank that supports disaster risk management projects worldwide. GFDRR supports countries to implement their commitments under the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (SFDRR), the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and the Paris Agreement.
records.intermediaries: The Facility is managed by the World Bank. GFDRR mobilizes grants from donor partners and channels them through World Bank Task Teams that work directly with government agencies, development partners, technical bodies, NGOs and private actors.
records.implementers: GFDRR, together with the World Bank Group, works with various partners on diaster risk management, including universities, the insurance sector, the risk-modeling industry, civil society organizations, foundations, technical and development agencies of national governments, the United Nations, and bilateral and multilateral institutions.
records.capital: Blended, mostly public. Donors include countries (Australia, Austria, Canada, European Union, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States) and philanthropies (Gates Foundation).
records.countries: Low and middle-income countries. Priority Core Countries: Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Ghana, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Senegal, Togo, Indonesia, Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vietnam, Kyrgyzstan, Haiti, Panama, Djibouti, Yemen, and Nepal
records.frequency: GFDRR has a demand- driven model, linking country needs with technical expertise, financing, and partnerships.
records.size: Grants are typically one to three years in duration. In fiscal year 2025, GFDRR supported over 100 countries through 328 grants, with a total value of USD 140.5 million.
records.initiative: The Global Program on Nature-Based Solutions for Climate Resilience (GPNBS), a thematic area of the GFDRR, is dedicated to expanding NBS investments across World Bank projects and sectors.
records.thematic: disaster risk and resilience, nature-based solutions, climate change adaptation
records.targetGroups: national and subnational governments, local communities
records.activities:
GFDRR's work spans the following priority areas:
- Strengthening Risk-Informed Decision Making (Priority 1)
- Reducing Risk and Mainstreaming DRM (Priority 2): Promotes safe, green, and inclusive built environments by investing in resilient infrastructure (transport, energy), housing, nature-based solutions, and urban resilience.
   - NBS include adaptive interventions to protect, manage, and/or restore natural or modified systems, including coastlines, cities, watersheds, and rivers, addressing multiple sustainable development goals, such as climate and disaster-risk resilience; economic and social prosperity; water security; and health and food security
- Enhancing Financial Preparedness (Priority 3)
- Improving Disaster Preparedness and Resilient Recovery (Priority 4)

Microfinance institutions
Financial intermediaries

Micro-entrepreneurs
Small businesses

NGOs
CSOs
Universities
Think tanks
Research institutes

SMEs
